Scrolling and Attention (Jakob Nielsen's Original Research Study) - NN/G

Skip to content

September Exclusive | Buy 2, Get 1 Free on Live Online Courses

Summary: Web users spend 80% of their time looking at information above the page fold. Although users do scroll, only 20% of their attention goes to content below the fold.

Update: With newer data from eyetracking on bigger monitors. In web design, there's much confusion about the " page fold" concept and the importance of keeping the most salient information within a page's initially-viewable area. (That is, in fact, the definition: "above the fold" simply means "viewable without further action.")

## In This Article:

- History of Page Fold
- Today’s Users Do Scroll, But Page-Length Considerations Still Apply
- Eyetracking Data
- Attention Focused at the Top
- Scrolling Behaviors
- Design Implications

## History of Page Fold

During the internet's early years, users often didn't scroll web pages at all. They simply looked at the visible information and used it to determine whether to stay or leave. Thus, in usability studies during that period (1994–1996), sites often failed if they placed important information below the fold, as most users didn't see it.

This reluctance to scroll made sense at the time because people were used to having computers show all their choices. Dialog boxes, CD-ROM multimedia shows, and HyperCard stacks all worked that way and didn't require scrolling. (Although users sometimes encountered scrolling text fields, they didn't need scrolling to see the commands and options and could thus make all decisions from the visible info.)

In 1997, however, I retracted the guideline to avoid scrolling pages because users had acclimated to scrolling on the web. This was a rare case in which a usability guideline changed quickly. Typically, usability guidelines are stable for many years: 80% of web usability guidelines from the 1990s are still in force.

## Today’s Users Do Scroll, But Page-Length Considerations Still Apply

Today, users will scroll. However, you still shouldn't ignore the fold and create super-long pages for two reasons:

- Long pages continue to be problematic because of users' limited attention span. People prefer sites that get to the point and let them get things done quickly. Besides the basic reluctance to read more words, scrolling is extra work.
- The real estate above the fold is more valuable than stuff below the fold for attracting and keeping users' attention.

So, yes, you can put information below the fold rather than limit yourself to bite-sized pages.

In fact, if you have a long article, it's better to present it as one scrolling page than to split it across multiple pageviews. Scrolling beats paging because it's easier for users to simply keep going down the page than it is to decide whether to click through for the next page of a fragmented article. (Saying that scrolling is easier obviously assumes a design that follows the guidelines for scrollbars and such.) Infinite scrolling is not always the answer either, however.

But no, the fact that users scroll doesn't free you from prioritizing and making sure that anything truly important remains above the fold.

Information-foraging theory says that people decide whether to continue along a path (including a scrolling path down a page) based on the current content's information scent. In other words, users will scroll below the fold only if the information above makes them believe the rest of the page will be valuable.

## Eyetracking Data

In 2010, we conducted a broad eyetracking study of user behavior across a wide variety of sites. To investigate whether the "fold" continues to be relevant, I analyzed parts of the study with a total of 57,453 fixations (instances when users look at something on a page, typically for less than half a second).

To avoid bias, I analyzed data from only 21 users accessing 541 different web pages, even though our full study was much larger. To convince you that I didn't limit the data for nefarious reasons, let me explain why I excluded some parts of the study from the present analysis.

Because our research goal was to generate fresh insights for our annual conference seminars, we targeted large parts of the study to test:

- sites with novel navigation features for the IA courses
- corporate blogs, interesting FAQs, and so on for the courses on Writing for the Web
- web-based apps for the Application Design seminar.

For each specialized topic, it's perfectly valid to test sites that have the features we want to investigate. For example, to gain insight into carousels we should track users' eyes as they encounter carousels. To do this, we simply ask them to use a site that happens to include a carousel, but we don't draw their attention to that design element.

When we deliberately ask people to test sites that contain particular design elements, we can't conclude that their behavior is representative of average sites. Sticking with the carousel example, people might well scroll less often than normal if the carousel successfully keeps their attention on the upper part of the page.

Our study also featured a component that let users go to any site they wanted. These nonconstrained tasks are the source of the data I analyzed because they tested regular websites people use, as opposed to sites we picked for their specific design features.

## Attention Focused at the Top

The following chart shows the distribution of user fixations along stripes that were 100 pixels tall. The bars represent total gaze time, as opposed to the number of fixations. (In other words, two fixations of 200 ms count the same as one fixation of 400 ms.)

Even though 5% of users' total time is spent past the 2,000-pixel mark, they tend to scan information that far from the top fairly superficially: some pages are very long (often 4,000+ pixels in my sample), and thus this 5% of user attention is spread very thinly.

In our study, user viewing time was distributed as follows:

- Above the fold: 80.3%
- Below the fold: 19.7%

For this study, we used a screen resolution of 1,024 × 768 pixels. These days, many users have somewhat bigger screens, and we've conducted many (noneyetracking) usability studies with larger resolutions. Although using a bigger monitor wouldn't change my conclusions, it would somewhat increase the percentage of user attention spent above the fold simply because more info would be available in the initially viewable space.

## Scrolling Behaviors

Sometimes, users do read down an entire page. It does happen. Rarely.

More commonly, we see one of the two behaviors illustrated in the following gaze plots.

Gaze plots showing where three users looked while visiting pages during three different tasks (one test participant per page) (Each blue dot represents one fixation, with bigger dots indicating longer viewing time.)

The left gaze plot also illustrates another point: the last element in a list often attracts additional attention. The first few items are definitely the most important, but the final item gets more views than the one before it. (That's also why the bar chart shows more attention to the 701–800 pixel area than to the 601–700 pixel area: the bottom of our study monitor fell within the former area.) The end of a list's importance is further enhanced by the recency effect, which says that the last thing a person sees remains particularly salient in the mind. (We discuss the design implications of the recency and primacy effects in our seminar on The Human Mind and Usability.)

The two other gaze plots show more common scrolling behaviors: intense viewing of the top of the page, moderate viewing of the middle, and fairly superficial viewing of the bottom. (I picked examples where users scrolled more or less all the way down — often there's no viewing of the bottom because users don't scroll that far.)

It's as if users arrive at a page with a certain amount of fuel in their tanks. As they "drive" down the page, they use up gas, and, sooner or later, they run dry. The amount of gas in the tank will vary, depending on each user's inherent motivation and interest in each page's specific topic. Also, the "gasoline" might evaporate or be topped up if content down the page is less or more relevant than the user expected.

In any case, user attention eventually peters out, and the further down the page users go, the less time they generally spend on each additional information unit.

The middle gaze plot shows a category page with 50 sofas:

- The top 2 rows get about 5–10 fixations per sofa.
- The next 4 rows get around 2–4 fixations per sofa.
- The next 8 rows typically get 1 fixation per sofa.
- The bottom 3 rows get 2 fixations for one sofa and no fixations for the remaining 7 sofas.

This is only a rough pattern, and users will deviate depending on the content. For example, the Cameon Loveseat and the Custom Hugo Loveseat both get 4 fixations despite being 2,750 pixels down the page. Presumably, the user found these two sofas particularly appealing.

## Design Implications

The implications are clear: the material that's the most important for the users' goals or your business goals should be above the fold. Users do look below the fold, but not nearly as much as they look above the fold.

People will look very far down a page if (a) the layout encourages scanning, and (b) the initially viewable information makes them believe that it will be worth their time to scroll.

## Summary
Across the provided sources, several popular marketing “facts” lack traceable primary evidence. The widely repeated “8‑second human attention span” has no primary study behind it; journalism could not verify the cited institutions ever produced such a finding, and multiple sources label it a myth [1][2][3][4][7]. Eye‑tracking research from Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g) shows users do scroll, but devote about 80% of their attention to content above the fold and 20% below it—undercutting “nobody scrolls” while quantifying the above‑the‑fold advantage [6]. Claims that “people read only 20% of a web page” are not supported in these sources; the 20% figure refers to attention below the fold in NN/g’s data, not the fraction of a page read [6]. For personalized email subject lines, Mailchimp advises they may increase open rates but provides no specific percentage uplift in this benchmark resource [8]. The “$300 million button” anecdote, A/B testing power/replication problems, and the base rate for non‑replicating “wins” are not addressed in the provided materials.

## Key Findings
- Human attention span “8 seconds” claim
  - Investigative journalism traced the oft‑cited references (NCBI/US National Library of Medicine and the Associated Press) and found no record of research backing the statistic; the listed sources could not locate any such study [7].
  - Multiple analyses characterize the “8‑second attention span” as a myth lacking scientific basis [1][2][3][4].
    - [1] explicitly calls the 8‑second claims “scientifically baseless.”
    - [2][3][4] describe the number as widely repeated without a primary source.

- Scrolling behavior and “below the fold”
  - NN/g original research (eyetracking) finds users “spend 80% of their time looking at information above the page fold” and “only 20% of their attention goes to content below the fold.” Users do scroll, but attention is concentrated above the fold. The article notes an update with newer eyetracking data on bigger monitors [6].

- “People read only 20% of a web page”
  - None of the provided sources support this specific claim. The only 20% figure identified is NN/g’s estimate of attention share below the fold, which is not the same as “reading only 20% of a page” [6].

- Personalized email subject lines
  - Mailchimp’s benchmark guidance: “Personalized emails may increase open rates for most users,” with practical advice to use merge tags in subject lines; no specific percentage uplift is claimed in this source [8].

- Practical steps implied by the evidence in these sources
  - Prioritize critical content above the fold because that region receives about 80% of users’ attention; still design for scrolling since users do scroll and allocate the remaining 20% of attention below the fold [6].
  - If testing email subject lines, personalization (e.g., merge tags for name/location) is a reasonable tactic to try; do not assume a fixed uplift without testing your audience, because this source gives no percentage benchmark [8].
  - Regarding attention‑span narratives, avoid using the 8‑second figure in strategy decks; none of these sources provide a primary study supporting it [1][2][3][4][7].

- Topics not evidenced in the provided sources
  - The “$300 million button” story: no coverage here of its provenance or whether it was a controlled experiment.
  - Replication/statistical power in commercial A/B testing and the frequency with which reported conversion “wins” fail to replicate: not covered in these sources.

## Evidence Quality
- Peer‑reviewed evidence
  - None of the supplied items are peer‑reviewed journal articles. No primary, peer‑reviewed study supporting an “8‑second attention span” is provided; one source explicitly labels that claim baseless [1], and another documents failed attempts to verify the cited institutions [7].

- Industry research and journalism
  - NN/g eyetracking: original UX research from a well‑known consultancy; not peer‑reviewed but primary observational data with quantified attention by fold position (80% vs 20%) and an update note for newer data on larger monitors [6].
  - BBC News report: investigative journalism that contacted the purported institutional sources of the 8‑second claim (NCBI/NLM and AP) and found no record, supporting the conclusion that the statistic lacks provenance [7].

- Agency/vendor/independent commentary
  - [1][2][3][4] critique the 8‑second claim; these are expert or practitioner commentaries (including an academic Substack), not peer‑reviewed studies.
  - Mailchimp benchmarks are practitioner guidance without a stated effect size for subject‑line personalization [8].

Given these materials, the consensus across commentary and journalism is that the 8‑second claim has no primary source; the strongest quantitative, primary evidence provided here concerns scrolling attention allocation (80/20 by fold) from NN/g [6]. No provided source quantifies a fixed uplift for personalized subject lines, and none address the $300M button anecdote or A/B test replication rates.

## Open Questions
- What is the original, citable primary study (if any) behind the “8‑second attention span” claim? None is identified in these sources [1][2][3][4][7].
- What are the detailed methods and sample characteristics behind NN/g’s 80/20 fold attention estimates (e.g., tasks, sites, sample sizes), and how do results vary by device? The article summary provides topline findings and notes an update but not full methodological detail here [6].
- Is there peer‑reviewed evidence quantifying the average percentage of a web page read (distinct from attention share by fold)? Not addressed in these sources.
- Do large‑scale, peer‑reviewed or audited datasets report a specific average uplift for personalized email subject lines, and under what conditions? Not addressed in these sources; Mailchimp gives no fixed percentage [8].
- What is the provenance and experimental design (observational vs controlled) of the “$300 million button” case? Not covered here.
- How often do reported A/B test wins fail to replicate in commercial practice, and what are the typical power/false positive rates? Not covered in these sources.
